claim: Bacteria within the gut microbiota possess the ability to metabolize a wide array of human drugs, foods, and toxins.
source: Bacteria within the gut microbiota possess the ability to metabolize a wide array of human drugs, foods, and toxins, but the responsible enzymes for these chemical events remain largely uncharacterized due to the time-consuming nature of current experimental approaches.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial metabolic capabilities in the gut microbiome, supported by the broader scientific literature and context of the manuscript.

claim: The responsible enzymes for chemical transformations by gut bacteria remain largely uncharacterized due to the time-consuming nature of current experimental approaches.
source: Bacteria within the gut microbiota possess the ability to metabolize a wide array of human drugs, foods, and toxins, but the responsible enzymes for these chemical events remain largely uncharacterized due to the time-consuming nature of current experimental approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rationale for developing SIMMER and the discussion of experimental limitations.

claim: Previous computational attempts to predict bacterial species and enzymes responsible for chemical transformations in the gut environment had low accuracy due to minimal chemical representation and sequence similarity search schemes.
source: Attempts have been made in the past to computationally predict which bacterial species and enzymes are responsible for chemical transformations in the gut environment, but with low accuracy due to minimal chemical representation and sequence similarity search schemes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison to existing methods (DrugBug and MicrobeFDT) presented later in the manuscript.

claim: SIMMER accurately predicts the responsible species and enzymes for a queried reaction, unlike previous methods.
source: We show that SIMMER accurately predicts the responsible species and enzymes for a queried reaction, unlike previous methods.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation data presented in the manuscript, including the MTX case study and comparison to existing methods.

claim: SIMMER predicted previously uncharacterized enzymes for 88 drug transformations known to occur in the human gut.
source: We demonstrate SIMMER use cases in the context of drug metabolism by predicting previously uncharacterized enzymes for 88 drug transformations known to occur in the human gut.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 6 and related analysis.

claim: SIMMER predictions for methotrexate metabolism were validated in vitro across 42 bacterial strains.
source: for one reaction, methotrexate (MTX) hydrolysis, we characterized human gut microbiome bacterial metabolism in vitro across 42 strains.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental HPLC data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Many bacterial enzymes are orthologous to the human metabolism repertoire, but many bacteria possess metabolic capabilities distinct from humans.
source: While some bacterial enzymes are orthologous to the human metabolism repertoire, many bacteria possess metabolic capabilities distinct from our own (Zimmermann et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zimmermann et al., 2019a.

claim: Microbial capacity for chemical transformation has implications for the bioavailability, toxicity, and efficacy of compounds humans ingest.
source: It is important to ascertain the extent of microbial capacity for chemical transformation because it has implications for the bioavailability, toxicity, and efficacy of the compounds humans ingest (Koppel et al., 2017; Spanogiannopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koppel et al., 2017 and Spanogiannopoulos et al., 2016.

claim: The human gut microbiome differs from individual to individual.
source: Additionally, because the human gut microbiome differs from individual to individual, knowledge of the prevalence and abundance of bacterial enzymes must be determined before beneficial clinical and dietary decisions can be made (Javdan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Javdan et al., 2020 and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The scientific community lacks genetic tools for nearly all bacterial species of the human microbiota.
source: While experimental methods can be employed to expand what we know of bacterial enzymatic capabilities in the gut, the scientific community lacks genetic tools for nearly all bacterial species of the human microbiota, and heterologous expression in model organisms can fail for a plethora of reasons (Bisanz et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bisanz et al., 2020 and Patel et al., 2022.

claim: Heterologous expression in model organisms can fail for a plethora of reasons.
source: While experimental methods can be employed to expand what we know of bacterial enzymatic capabilities in the gut, the scientific community lacks genetic tools for nearly all bacterial species of the human microbiota, and heterologous expression in model organisms can fail for a plethora of reasons (Bisanz et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bisanz et al., 2020 and Patel et al., 2022.

claim: When experimental methods are tractable, the time required is often so extended that knowledge is gained in a low-throughput manner.
source: When experimental methods are tractable, the time required is often so extended that knowledge is gained in a low-throughput manner.
evidence: This is a general observation about experimental limitations in the field.

claim: Two previously published methods aimed to predict known drug metabolism events within the human gut microbiome but had limited accuracy.
source: Two previously published methods aimed to predict known drug metabolism events within the human gut microbiome, but the accuracy of their species and enzyme predictions was limited due to the fact that both tools only consider substrates, rather than a full chemical description of substrate(s), cofactor(s), and product(s) formed in a reaction (Guthrie et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guthrie et al., 2019 and Sharma et al., 2017, and is validated by the comparison data in the manuscript.

claim: Previous methods only consider substrates, rather than a full chemical description of substrate(s), cofactor(s), and product(s) formed in a reaction.
source: Two previously published methods aimed to predict known drug metabolism events within the human gut microbiome, but the accuracy of their species and enzyme predictions was limited due to the fact that both tools only consider substrates, rather than a full chemical description of substrate(s), cofactor(s), and product(s) formed in a reaction (Guthrie et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original methods and is confirmed by the authors' analysis.

claim: Previous methods were limited by the use of small databases that do not fully capture the diversity of the human gut microbiome.
source: Both tools were also limited by the use of small databases that do not fully capture the diversity of the human gut microbiome (Guthrie et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original methods and comparison of database sizes.

claim: SIMMER combines chemoinformatics and metagenomics approaches to predict bacterial species and enzymes capable of known biotransformations in the human gut.
source: To address these gaps in accurate predictive software, we present SIMMER, a tool that combines chemoinformatics and metagenomics approaches to accurately predict bacterial species and enzymes capable of known biotransformations in the human gut.
evidence: This describes the methodology of SIMMER as presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: SIMMER predicts specific bacterial enzyme sequences responsible for a given input reaction.
source: Given an input reaction, SIMMER predicts specific bacterial enzyme sequences responsible for the transformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the manuscript with various examples.

claim: Each SIMMER predicted sequence is annotated with taxonomy, potential function, and prevalence/abundance in human metagenomic samples.
source: Each predicted sequence is annotated with taxonomy, potential function, and prevalence/abundance in human metagenomic samples.
evidence: This is shown in the output data and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: SIMMER uses full chemical representations that include cofactors employed and products produced in a reaction.
source: Our key innovations are the use of full chemical representations that include cofactors employed and products produced in a reaction, the use of statistically informed sequence searches of a comprehensive human gut microbiome gene catalog, and the development of an enzyme class predictor based on reaction rather than gene sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the methods and validated by comparison to methods using only substrates.

claim: SIMMER uses statistically informed sequence searches of a comprehensive human gut microbiome gene catalog.
source: Our key innovations are the use of full chemical representations that include cofactors employed and products produced in a reaction, the use of statistically informed sequence searches of a comprehensive human gut microbiome gene catalog, and the development of an enzyme class predictor based on reaction rather than gene sequence.
evidence: This is described in the methods section with details about pHMM searches of the UHGG database.

claim: SIMMER developed an enzyme class predictor based on reaction rather than gene sequence.
source: Our key innovations are the use of full chemical representations that include cofactors employed and products produced in a reaction, the use of statistically informed sequence searches of a comprehensive human gut microbiome gene catalog, and the development of an enzyme class predictor based on reaction rather than gene sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and the EC prediction methodology.

claim: SIMMER identified the likely bacterial enzyme for 88 drugs known to be metabolized by the gut microbiome for which the enzyme was previously unknown.
source: we identify the likely bacterial enzyme for 88 drugs known to be metabolized by the gut microbiome for which the enzyme was previously unknown.
evidence: This is presented in Figure 6 and related analysis.

claim: SIMMER's underlying data were drawn from the MetaCyc reaction database.
source: SIMMER's underlying data were drawn from the MetaCyc reaction database because its small-molecule reaction descriptions each possess at least one experimentally validated enzyme annotation and because it is currently the most comprehensive database of its kind (Altman et al., 2013; Caspi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2013 and Caspi et al., 2020.

claim: MetaCyc small-molecule reaction descriptions each possess at least one experimentally validated enzyme annotation.
source: SIMMER's underlying data were drawn from the MetaCyc reaction database because its small-molecule reaction descriptions each possess at least one experimentally validated enzyme annotation and because it is currently the most comprehensive database of its kind (Altman et al., 2013; Caspi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2013 and Caspi et al., 2020.

claim: MetaCyc is currently the most comprehensive database of its kind.
source: SIMMER's underlying data were drawn from the MetaCyc reaction database because its small-molecule reaction descriptions each possess at least one experimentally validated enzyme annotation and because it is currently the most comprehensive database of its kind (Altman et al., 2013; Caspi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2013 and Caspi et al., 2020.

claim: SIMMER created two-dimensional fingerprint representations for 8914 enzyme-driven reactions in MetaCyc.
source: To build a precomputed chemical search space for SIMMER queries (Figure 1A), we created two-dimensional fingerprint representations for 8914 enzyme-driven reactions in MetaCyc (Caspi et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1.

claim: SIMMER estimated the similarity between all pairs of reactions based on Tanimoto coefficients.
source: Using these fingerprints, we estimated the similarity between all pairs of reactions based on Tanimoto coefficients.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: SIMMER compiled Uniprot and/or Entrez gene identifiers linked to each MetaCyc transformation into a profile hidden Markov model (pHMM).
source: To build the enzyme backbone of SIMMER, we compiled the Uniprot and/or Entrez gene identifiers linked to each MetaCyc transformation into a profile hidden Markov model (pHMM) that represents the diversity of the enzyme family for a respective reaction.
evidence: This is described in the methods section.

claim: The pHMMs were used to query the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG) collection of 286,997 isolate genomes and metagenome assembled genomes from the human gut environment.
source: The resulting pHMMs were then used to query the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG) collection of 286,997 isolate genomes and metagenome assembled genomes from the human gut environment (Almeida et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Almeida et al., 2021.

claim: Prevalence and abundance of all pHMM search hits were assessed in stool metagenomes from the PREDICT human cohort using MIDAS2.
source: Additionally, prevalence and abundance of all pHMM search hits were assessed in stool metagenomes from the PREDICT human cohort using MIDAS2, an implementation of Metagenomic Intra-Species Diversity Analysis System (MIDAS) designed for use with the UHGG catalog (Almeida et al., 2021; Nayfach et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2021; Nayfach et al., 2016; and Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: SIMMER predicts an Enzyme Commission (EC) code that describes the chemical nature of the query.
source: As an auxiliary function to enzyme sequence prediction, SIMMER additionally predicts an Enzyme Commission (EC) code that describes the chemical nature of the query.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and throughout the results.

claim: EC codes are four-digit identifiers of enzyme-driven reactions, where each digit describes the reaction with increasing chemical granularity.
source: EC codes are four-digit identifiers of enzyme-driven reactions, where each digit describes the reaction with increasing chemical granularity (McDonald et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McDonald et al., 2009 and is established knowledge.

claim: The first digit of an EC code, the EC class, describes broad chemistry such as whether the reaction is an oxidoreduction, hydrolysis, etc. event.
source: The first digit, the EC class, describes broad chemistry such as whether the reaction is an oxidoreduction, hydrolysis, etc. event.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC nomenclature.

claim: The second and third digits of an EC code, the EC sub-class and sub-sub-class, describe more detailed chemical information such as electron donor or transfer group identity.
source: The second and third digits, the EC sub-class and sub-sub-class, describe more detailed chemical information such as electron donor or transfer group identity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC nomenclature.

claim: The fourth and final digit of an EC code, the EC serial designation, often describes a reaction's specific substrate(s).
source: The fourth and final digit, the EC serial designation, often describes a reaction's specific substrate(s).
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC nomenclature.

claim: SIMMER implemented a novel method to predict EC codes by extending a common approach to gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
source: We implemented and validated a novel method to predict EC codes by extending a common approach to gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Subramanian et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Subramanian et al., 2005 and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: SIMMER predicted reaction types for queries with high recall and accuracy for EC classes, sub-classes, and sub-sub-classes.
source: With this enrichment method, SIMMER predicted reaction types for queries with high recall and accuracy for EC classes, sub-classes, and sub-sub-classes (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B and related supplementary figures.

claim: SIMMER groups similar reactions together in chemical space.
source: SIMMER clusters similar reactions together in chemical space.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A.

claim: For all EC classes, scores were smaller within versus without EC classes using SIMMER's chemical representation, indicating that SIMMER can detect reaction similarity within EC classes.
source: For all EC classes, scores were smaller within versus without EC classes using SIMMER's chemical representation, indicating that SIMMER can detect reaction similarity within EC classes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: SIMMER's ability to group similar reactions in chemical space is resilient to different fingerprinting methods.
source: We determined that SIMMER's ability to group similar reactions in chemical space is resilient to different fingerprinting methods (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), but not to loss of products created and cofactors consumed in a reaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: SIMMER's ability to group similar reactions in chemical space is not resilient to loss of products created and cofactors consumed in a reaction.
source: We determined that SIMMER's ability to group similar reactions in chemical space is resilient to different fingerprinting methods (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), but not to loss of products created and cofactors consumed in a reaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Similar reactions only cluster together in chemical space when a full reaction description (i.e., SIMMER's representation method) is employed.
source: Thus, we showed that similar reactions only cluster together in chemical space when a full reaction description (i.e., SIMMER's representation method) is employed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of different chemical representations in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: SIMMER predicted high similarity between reactions conducted by a shared enzyme, and low similarity for those reactions without a shared enzyme.
source: SIMMER predicted high similarity between reactions conducted by a shared enzyme, and low similarity for those reactions without a shared enzyme (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a negative association between chemical reaction distance and global sequence similarity of MetaCyc enzyme annotations, though there is much variation in this relationship.
source: We also found a negative association between chemical reaction distance and global sequence similarity of MetaCyc enzyme annotations, though there is much variation in this relationship (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B.

claim: MetaCyc reactions with identical chemical representations could be conducted by proteins with only ~20% global percent identity all the way to 100%.
source: Indeed, MetaCyc reactions with identical chemical representations could be conducted by proteins with only ~20% global percent identity all the way to 100% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relationship between sequence similarity and similarity in chemical function reflects the known association between these properties, as well as reports that this relationship can often be overestimated.
source: This reflects the known association between sequence similarity and similarity in chemical function, as well as reports that this relationship can often be overestimated (Tian and Skolnick, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tian and Skolnick, 2003.

claim: 300 drug metabolism events associated with the human gut microbiome were curated from the literature.
source: First, we curated 300 drug metabolism events associated with the human gut microbiome from the literature (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is described in the methods and results sections.

claim: For 33 of the curated reactions, the responsible bacterial enzyme, characterized metabolite(s), and associated EC annotation are known.
source: For 33 of these reactions the responsible bacterial enzyme, characterized metabolite(s), and associated EC annotation are known (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is described in the methods and used as positive controls.

claim: The 33 characterized reactions are conducted by 18 enzymes.
source: These 33 reactions are conducted by 18 enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and used to create the expanded database.

claim: An expanded database of the 18 characterized enzymes from pHMM and phmmer searches of the UHGG database yielded 52,849 total candidate homologs (a median of 1087 candidates per enzyme).
source: To account for this, we created an expanded database (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 1) of the 18 characterized enzymes from pHMM and phmmer searches of the UHGG database (Almeida et al., 2021), yielding 52,849 total candidate homologs (a median of 1087 candidates per enzyme).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After filtering enzymes by various criteria, the expanded database contained a median of 2 high-confidence homologous sequences per enzyme (range = 0–460 across the 18 enzyme families).
source: After filtering enzymes by hmmer significance, alignment length, presence in data from the human jejunum (Zmora et al., 2018) and RNA-sequencing studies (Integrative HMP (iHMP) Research Network Consortium, 2019), and predicted affinity for the substrate in question using the Similarity Ensemble Approach (Keiser et al., 2007), our database contained a median of 2 high-confidence homologous sequences per enzyme (range = 0–460 across the 18 enzyme families, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and described in the text with citations.

claim: 741 additional enzyme sequences for 33 reactions formed an expanded testing set of known gut bacterial enzymes.
source: These 741 additional enzyme sequences for 33 reactions formed an expanded testing set of known gut bacterial enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and used for validation.

claim: Only 3 of the 33 positive control reactions are themselves MetaCyc entries (5-ASA, dopamine, and levodopa degradation).
source: Only 3 of these 33 reactions are themselves MetaCyc entries (5-ASA, dopamine, and levodopa degradation); if enzymes of reactions not described in MetaCyc were also accurately predicted, it would show that SIMMER can discover non-identical yet chemically similar reactions.
evidence: This is stated in the text to demonstrate SIMMER's ability to predict beyond exact matches.

claim: In 29 cases (88%), the characterized enzyme(s) for a reaction was found in the output enzyme list for the top 20 of the ranked MetaCyc reactions.
source: In 29 cases (88%), the characterized (i.e., positive control) enzyme(s) for a reaction was found in the output enzyme list for the top 20 of the ranked MetaCyc reactions (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and represents SIMMER's accuracy.

claim: The top 20 out of ~9000 reactions was chosen as an accuracy cutoff because this was the median rank of a true positive reaction in the analysis of MetaCyc reactions conducted by the same enzyme.
source: We chose the top 20 out of ~9000 reactions as an accuracy cutoff, because this was the median rank of a true positive reaction in our analysis of MetaCyc reactions conducted by the same enzyme (Figure 3A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is justified by reference to Figure 3A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The positive controls span four EC classes (EC1 oxidoreductases, EC2 transferases, EC3 hydrolases, and EC4 lyases).
source: Since the positive controls span four EC classes (EC1 oxidoreductases, EC2 transferases, EC3 hydrolases, and EC4 lyases), this result demonstrates SIMMER's ability to accurately predict microbiome-based enzymes for a diversity of reaction types.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: Despite inaccurate EC predictions for nicardipine reduction and brivudine transformation, SIMMER was able to predict AzoR and BT_4554 enzymes as responsible for the reactions.
source: Also, despite inaccurate EC predictions for nicardipine reduction and brivudine transformation, SIMMER was able to, respectively, predict AzoR and BT_4554 enzymes as responsible for the reactions, because enzyme and EC predictions are separately computed by SIMMER (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and demonstrates the independence of enzyme and EC predictions.

claim: For 28 out of the 30 reactions with EC annotations, SIMMER's top EC class prediction was correct.
source: For five queries SIMMER predicted more than one significant EC class, but for 28 out of the 30 reactions (including these five), SIMMER's top EC class prediction was correct (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The two failed EC predictions were for nicardipine reduction (inappropriately predicted as an isomerase reaction) and for brivudine transformation (for which SIMMER made no significant prediction).
source: The two failed EC predictions were for nicardipine reduction (inappropriately predicted as an isomerase reaction) and for brivudine transformation (for which SIMMER made no significant prediction).
evidence: This is stated in the text as the exceptions to SIMMER's EC prediction accuracy.

claim: DrugBug had 37% accuracy in predicting EC classes for the 30 EC annotated positive control reactions (in comparison to SIMMER's 93%).
source: For the 30 EC annotated positive control reactions, DrugBug had 37% accuracy in predicting EC classes (in comparison to SIMMER's 93%) and predicted the correct enzyme for only a single reaction, SN38 glucuronide deconjugation, despite the presence of chemically similar reactions metabolized by the same enzyme amongst the positive controls (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and represents a direct comparison.

claim: DrugBug predicted the correct enzyme for only a single reaction, SN38 glucuronide deconjugation.
source: For the 30 EC annotated positive control reactions, DrugBug had 37% accuracy in predicting EC classes (in comparison to SIMMER's 93%) and predicted the correct enzyme for only a single reaction, SN38 glucuronide deconjugation, despite the presence of chemically similar reactions metabolized by the same enzyme amongst the positive controls (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1—source data 1.

claim: Both DrugBug and SIMMER were able to predict EC classes for sorivudine, but only SIMMER was able to accurately predict the specific enzyme (BT_4554) responsible for the drug's degradation.
source: Both DrugBug and SIMMER were able to predict EC classes for sorivudine, but only SIMMER was able to accurately predict the specific enzyme (BT_4554) responsible for the drug's degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the comparison to DrugBug.

claim: For ginsenoside Rb1, quercetin-3-glucoside, and cycasin, SIMMER accurately predicted EC codes with improved resolution over DrugBug.
source: For ginsenoside Rb1 (3.2.1.192), quercetin-3-glucoside (3.2.1.21), and cycasin (3.2.1.21), SIMMER accurately predicted EC codes out to sub-sub-class (3.2.1.-), serial designation (3.2.1.21), and sub-sub-class (3.2.1.-), respectively, which was a resolution improvement over DrugBug (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1—source data 1.

claim: MicrobeFDT produced EC predictions for 14 of the 30 positive controls, four of which were correct (29% accuracy).
source: We next queried the 30 EC annotated drug metabolism positive controls against MicrobeFDT, a chemical graph tool that only predicts EC codes, not enzyme sequences. MicrobeFDT produced EC predictions for 14 of the 30 positive controls, four of which were correct (29% accuracy).
evidence: This is stated in the comparison to MicrobeFDT.

claim: Neither DrugBug nor MicrobeFDT computed predictions for all 33 positive control reactions.
source: Neither DrugBug nor MicrobeFDT computed predictions for all 33 positive control reactions.
evidence: This is stated in the comparison section.

claim: MicrobeFDT made so few EC predictions (14/30) because it is reliant on a fixed chemical database that cannot be modified by the user.
source: MicrobeFDT made so few EC predictions (14/30) because it is reliant on a fixed chemical database that cannot be modified by the user, meaning that a compound cannot be queried if it is not already present in MicrobeFDT's graph.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of MicrobeFDT.

claim: DrugBug's protein database only contains information from 491 bacterial genomes (in comparison to SIMMER's 286,997 genomes).
source: While DrugBug does allow for novel chemical input, its protein database only contains information from 491 bacterial genomes (in comparison to SIMMER's 286,997 genomes), affecting its ability to make enzyme-specific predictions.
evidence: This is stated in the comparison and shown in Table 1.

claim: When SIMMER was modified to run with a chemical representation that includes only the substrate, enzyme prediction accuracy dropped from 88% down to 33%, and EC prediction accuracy dropped from 93% down to 48%.
source: To test if SIMMER's better performance could be attributed to including cofactors and products, we modified our code to run with a chemical representation that includes only the substrate of each positive control reaction. Enzyme prediction accuracy dropped from 88% down to 33%, and EC prediction accuracy dropped from 93% down to 48% (Table 1—source data 1), supporting the hypothesis that SIMMER's better performance when compared to DrugBug and MicrobeFDT is due in large part to our use of chemical representations that include the full reaction.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1—source data 1 and demonstrates the importance of full reaction representation.

claim: Of the 88 reactions queried, SIMMER determined significant EC predictions for 75 reactions (86.2%), and 61 (70.1%) of these were out to the serial designation (i.e., highest resolution) EC code.
source: Of the 88 reactions queried, SIMMER determined significant EC predictions for 75 reactions (86.2%), and 61 (70.1%) of these were out to the serial designation (i.e., highest resolution) EC code (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results for novel drug metabolism predictions.

claim: SIMMER's EC predictions resulted in expanded and diversified EC class membership for drug transformations known to occur in the microbiome.
source: SIMMER's EC predictions resulted in expanded and diversified EC class membership for drug transformations known to occur in the microbiome (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SIMMER predictions resulted in a large expansion of putative hydrolysis, reduction, and isomerization reactions in the human gut microbiome.
source: Of interest, this analysis resulted in a large expansion of putative hydrolysis, reduction, and isomerization reactions in the human gut microbiome.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The number of SIMMER predictions varies widely by reaction, with median output of 372 genes, 286 genomes, and 10 phyla predicted as responsible across the 88 reactions.
source: The number of SIMMER predictions varies widely by reaction, with median output of 372 genes, 286 genomes, and 10 phyla predicted as responsible across the 88 reactions (Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Oral MTX is an anti-folate immunosuppressant, and the first-line therapy for individuals with rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
source: Oral MTX is an anti-folate immunosuppressant, and the first-line therapy for individuals with rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: About half of RA patients show inadequate response to MTX.
source: About half of RA patients, however, show inadequate response to MTX (Scher et al., 2020), and the reasons for this remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scher et al., 2020.

claim: Oral bioavailability of MTX is subject to large inter-individual variation with values ranging from 32% to 70%.
source: This lack of efficacy may be due to altered pharmacokinetics, as oral bioavailability of MTX is subject to large inter-individual variation with values ranging from 32% to 70% (Roon and Laar, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roon and Laar, 2006.

claim: MTX is estimated to undergo extensive enterohepatic circulation, which results in increased exposure to gut bacteria in the small intestine.
source: MTX is estimated to undergo extensive enterohepatic circulation, which results in increased exposure to gut bacteria in the small intestine (Roon and Laar, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roon and Laar, 2006.

claim: MTX degrades to inactive metabolites 2,4-diamino-N10-methylpteroic acid (DAMPA) and glutamate in mice with intact gut microbiomes, but not in their antibiotic treated counterparts.
source: This exposure may result in MTX depletion, as it is known that MTX degrades to inactive metabolites 2,4-diamino-N10-methylpteroic acid (DAMPA) and glutamate in mice with intact gut microbiomes, but not in their antibiotic treated counterparts (Zaharko et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zaharko et al., 1969.

claim: In a recent human study, ex vivo stool samples from MTX non-responders depleted MTX to a higher degree.
source: In a recent human study, ex vivo stool samples from MTX non-responders depleted MTX to a higher degree, though the relevant strains and enzymes were not determined (Artacho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Artacho et al., 2021.

claim: When queried with MTX and its gut bacteria associated metabolites DAMPA and glutamate, SIMMER calculated a most similar MetaCyc reaction (3.4.17.11-RXN) and a significant EC prediction (3.4.17.11, p-value <0.001).
source: When queried with MTX and its gut bacteria associated metabolites DAMPA and glutamate, SIMMER calculated a most similar MetaCyc reaction (3.4.17.11-RXN) and a significant EC prediction (3.4.17.11, p-value <0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the MTX case study results.

claim: The most similar MetaCyc reaction to MTX hydrolysis describes the hydrolysis of folate into pteroate and glutamate, driven by a glutamate carboxypeptidase (Cpg2) found in environmental Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: This MetaCyc reaction describes the hydrolysis of folate into pteroate and glutamate, driven by a glutamate carboxypeptidase (Cpg2) found in environmental Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
evidence: This is stated in the MTX case study results.

claim: Hydrolysis of MTX is chemically similar to hydrolysis of folate with a Tanimoto coefficient = 0.6, and normalized euclidean distance = 0.05 in SIMMER's precomputed chemical space.
source: Hydrolysis of MTX is chemically similar to hydrolysis of folate (Figure 7A) with a Tanimoto coefficient = 0.6, and normalized euclidean distance = 0.05 in SIMMER's precomputed chemical space.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and stated in the text.

claim: SIMMER made 2286 human gut microbiome enzyme predictions for degrading MTX into DAMPA and glutamate.
source: SIMMER made 2286 human gut microbiome enzyme predictions for degrading MTX into DAMPA and glutamate (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the MTX case study results.

claim: The most common Prokka annotation for SIMMER's MTX-metabolizing enzymes is Carboxypeptidase G2s.
source: The most common Prokka annotation for these enzymes is Carboxypeptidase G2s (Figure 7B) due to their sequence similarity to MetaCyc's environmental Cpg2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SIMMER's predicted MTX-metabolizing enzymes had a median global identity of 33% to Pseudomonas sp. RS-16 Cpg2, an enzyme known to conduct hydrolysis of MTX.
source: Furthermore, SIMMER's predicted enzymes had a median global identity of 33% to Pseudomonas sp. RS-16 (an environmental bacterium) Cpg2, an enzyme known to conduct hydrolysis of MTX (Larimer et al., 2014; Jeyaharan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larimer et al., 2014 and Jeyaharan et al., 2016.

claim: MTX depletion varied across the strain collection, with 10 isolates exhibiting at least a 50% decrease in MTX levels compared to control.
source: MTX depletion varied across the strain collection, with 10 isolates exhibiting at least a 50% decrease in MTX levels compared to control.
evidence: This is stated in the experimental validation results.

claim: There was a statistically significant concordance between SIMMER's predictions of which strains had an enzyme capable of metabolizing MTX and experimental results (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 5.4, p-value <0.05).
source: There was a statistically significant concordance between SIMMER's predictions of which strains had an enzyme capable of metabolizing MTX and our experimental results (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio = 5.4, p-value <0.05, Figure 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 with statistical analysis.

claim: E. coli BW25113 possesses the multidrug resistance efflux pump AcrAB-TolC, which actively exports MTX.
source: One of these discordant strains, E. coli BW25113, possesses the multidrug resistance efflux pump AcrAB-TolC, which actively exports MTX (Kopytek et al., 2000), explaining why MTX was not affected.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kopytek et al., 2000.

claim: 3/7 SIMMER predictions that did not match experimental results could be explained by the ability of drug efflux to mask the potential for enzymatic activity.
source: Thus, 3/7 SIMMER predictions that did not match experimental results could be explained by the ability of drug efflux to mask the potential for enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for discordant results.

claim: Both DrugBug and MicrobeFDT incorrectly predicted that MTX degradation is through transferases rather than hydrolases.
source: Both incorrectly predicted that MTX degradation is through transferases rather than hydrolases.
evidence: This is stated in the comparison for the MTX case study.

claim: Only SIMMER was able to significantly predict species capable of MTX metabolism (SIMMER odds ratio = 5.4 versus DrugBug odds ratio = 0).
source: We found that only SIMMER was able to significantly predict species capable of MTX metabolism (SIMMER odds ratio = 5.4 versus DrugBug odds ratio = 0).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: DrugBug produced zero true positives and predicted that MTX metabolism was a feature largely restricted to members of Bacteroidetes, a group who exhibited no activity in the in vitro assay.
source: DrugBug produced zero true positives and predicted that MTX metabolism was a feature largely restricted to members of Bacteroidetes, a group who exhibited no activity in our in vitro assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Of SIMMER's 2286 enzyme predictions for MTX hydrolysis, 386 were detected in the fecal samples of RA patients at baseline (prior to treatment).
source: Of SIMMER's 2286 enzyme predictions for MTX hydrolysis, 386 were detected in the fecal samples of RA patients at baseline (prior to treatment).
evidence: This is stated in the external validation results.

claim: MTX non-responders exhibited a significant enrichment of SIMMER MTX predictions in their stool samples.
source: MTX non-responders exhibited a significant enrichment of SIMMER MTX predictions in their stool samples (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant negative correlation was seen between patients' disease score improvements and abundance of SIMMER enzyme predictions.
source: Similarly, a significant negative correlation was seen between patients' disease score improvements and abundance of SIMMER enzyme predictions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B with statistical analysis.

claim: Dexamethasone was shown to be metabolized solely by Clostridium scindens (ATCC 35704) out of a collection of 76 isolates representative of the human gut microbiome.
source: Dexamethasone was recently shown to be metabolized solely by Clostridium scindens (ATCC 35704) out of a collection of 76 isolates representative of the human gut microbiome (Zimmermann et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zimmermann et al., 2019b.

claim: When dexamethasone metabolism was assessed in 28 shotgun sequenced human stool samples, metabolite formation varied substantially by individual, but could not be explained by C. scindens species abundance.
source: When the authors assessed dexamethasone metabolism in 28 shotgun sequenced human stool samples, metabolite formation varied substantially by individual, but could not be explained by C. scindens species abundance.
evidence: This is stated in reference to the Zimmermann et al., 2019b study.

claim: There was a significant association between metabolite formation and number of SIMMER enzyme aligned reads for dexamethasone metabolism.
source: We found a significant association between metabolite formation and number of SIMMER enzyme aligned reads, and also a significant association between parent compound consumption and number of SIMMER enzyme aligned reads (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B with statistical analysis.

claim: There was not a significant correlation between number of desAB reads and either metabolite formation or dexamethasone consumption slopes.
source: To ensure that SIMMER's enzyme prediction for dexamethasone cleavage was not enriched in metabolizing stool samples due to co-occurrence with already known DesAB, we next assessed the abundance of desAB reads across the 28 samples and found no significant correlation between number of reads and either metabolite formation or dexamethasone consumption slopes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIMMER enzyme predictions were directly found in the pilot donor stool sample for all eight of the reactions with identified metabolites from the Javdan et al. study.
source: Because shotgun metagenomics sequencing for the pilot donor was deposited, we were able to confirm via tBLASTn searches that SIMMER enzyme predictions were directly found in the pilot donor stool sample for all eight of the reactions with identified metabolites (Figure 10—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the external validation results.

claim: Donors who could metabolize a given drug possessed a significant enrichment of species predicted by SIMMER for five out of the six reactions analyzed from the Javdan et al. study.
source: We found that donors who could metabolize a given drug possessed a significant enrichment of species predicted by SIMMER. This was the case for five out of the six reactions analyzed (Figure 10—source data 1, Figure 10A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A.

claim: SIMMER is available as both a command-line tool and a web tool.
source: In addition to providing SIMMER (https://github.com/aebustion/SIMMER, copy archived at Bustion, 2023) as a command-line tool that quickly generates enzyme sequence predictions (fasta and tab-separated-value files), EC predictions (tab-separated-value file), and MetaCyc reactions ranked by similarity (tab-separated-value file) based on a user's input reaction, SIMMER is also available as a user-friendly website (https://simmer.pollard.gladstone.org/).
evidence: This is stated in the SIMMER software section.

claim: SIMMER's underlying chemical and protein databases will be updated whenever major releases of MetaCyc that result in new enzyme-annotated reactions are released (estimated to be once a year).
source: SIMMER's underlying chemical and protein databases will be updated whenever major releases of MetaCyc that result in new enzyme-annotated reactions are released (estimated to be once a year).
evidence: This is stated as a maintenance plan for SIMMER.

claim: MetaCyc is the largest annotated bacterial reaction database to date.
source: While MetaCyc is the largest annotated bacterial reaction database to date (Altman et al., 2013; Caspi et al., 2020), it likely only represents a fraction of the still underexplored microbiome catalyzed biotransformation space.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2013 and Caspi et al., 2020.

claim: MetaCyc likely only represents a fraction of the still underexplored microbiome catalyzed biotransformation space.
source: While MetaCyc is the largest annotated bacterial reaction database to date (Altman et al., 2013; Caspi et al., 2020), it likely only represents a fraction of the still underexplored microbiome catalyzed biotransformation space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: EC codes are not sufficient for predictions of microbiome orthologs due to the paucity of functional annotations in microbiome datasets.
source: To connect these chemical descriptions to bacterial proteins in the human gut, we knew it was important not to rely on EC codes (as previous methods have done) to find relevant enzyme sequences. While EC codes are helpful for describing reaction types, they are not sufficient for predictions of microbiome orthologs due to the paucity of functional annotations in microbiome datasets (Almeida et al., 2021; Thomas and Segata, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2021 and Thomas and Segata, 2019.

claim: About 36% of assigned EC numbers lack either a gene or protein sequence.
source: Even when present, EC entries are sometimes incomplete, with about 36% of assigned EC numbers lacking either a gene or protein sequence (Pouliot and Karp, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pouliot and Karp, 2007.

claim: EC nomenclature fails to adequately express the complexity of peptidase enzymes (EC 3.4, about 10% of the enzymes currently classified by EC).
source: Lastly, EC nomenclature fails to adequately express the complexity of peptidase enzymes (EC 3.4, about 10% of the enzymes currently classified by EC). All peptidases catalyze a nearly identical reaction, hydrolysis of a peptide bond, and as a result, the EC has lumped peptidases of diverse functions into only a few low-resolution sub-classes (McDonald and Tipton, 2023; McDonald and Tipton, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McDonald and Tipton, 2023 and McDonald and Tipton, 2014.

claim: pHMMs encode protein family evolutionary patterns present in a multiple sequence alignment.
source: This position-specific information can be leveraged by performing homology searches with pHMMs, which encode protein family evolutionary patterns present in a multiple sequence alignment (Eddy, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eddy, 1998 and is established knowledge about pHMMs.

claim: In the antibiotic resistance protein space, pHMMs that incorporate position-specific information have found distant homologs with retained function not recovered via pairwise search methods.
source: In the antibiotic resistance protein space, for example, pHMMs that incorporate position-specific information have found distant homologs with retained function not recovered via pairwise search methods (Gibson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gibson et al., 2015.

claim: Previous research has shown that global sequence identity does not necessarily map to similar function.
source: pHMM searches are an improvement over BLAST from the standpoint of finding distant homologs and from the standpoint of finding targets with retained activity, as previous research has shown that global sequence identity does not necessarily map to similar function (Gerlt et al., 2012; Koppel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerlt et al., 2012 and Koppel et al., 2018.

claim: pHMM methods can still be uncorrelated with functional similarity and SIMMER enzyme predictions will include many false positives and require experimental validation.
source: While an improvement, pHMM methods can still be uncorrelated with functional similarity and SIMMER enzyme predictions will include many false positives and require experimental validation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the method.

claim: The goal of SIMMER is to prioritize and limit the set of possible experiments one might do rather than to replace experiments.
source: The goal of SIMMER, therefore, is to prioritize and limit the set of possible experiments one might do rather than to replace experiments.
evidence: This is stated as the intended use of SIMMER.

claim: 13,387 gene-annotated, enzyme-driven bacterial reactions were downloaded from MetaCyc version 24.1.
source: 13,387 gene-annotated, enzyme-driven bacterial reactions were downloaded from MetaCyc version 24.1 (Caspi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: All MetaCyc compounds were protonated based on the pH environment of 7.4 in the human small intestine.
source: All MetaCyc compounds were then protonated based on the pH environment of 7.4 in the human small intestine, where most oral drug absorption occurs.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

source: Of the 13,387 MetaCyc reactions, 8914 were able to be fingerprinted using this method.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

source: Failed fingerprints were due to ambiguous SMILES identifiers or presence of non-small-molecule compounds in a reaction, such as peptides.
